overview.text: Revenue of $2,532m in the twelve months to 30 Jun 2026, flat on a year earlier; 18.19m paying users at $139.68 average revenue per user in Q2 2026.
GAAP operating income of $675m and depreciation and amortisation of $156m over the same twelve months, giving reported EBITDA of $830m (32.8% margin).

The history table uses Dropbox’s own statements. EBITDA is operating income plus D&A as reported, so FY2023 includes a $155m gain on real estate and FY2024 a heavier cost base before restructuring. Interest is the reported net figure: Dropbox earned more interest than it paid until the 2024 term loan, so FY2023 and FY2024 show negative figures (net interest income). Change in working capital is the sum of the working-capital lines in the cash flow statement, excluding leases.
overview.source: Dropbox Form 10-K for fiscal 2025 (income statement, cash flow statement and balance sheet)

overview.text: Stock-based pay of $304m over twelve months (12.0% of revenue). Dropbox’s non-GAAP operating margin of about 40% adds this back.
FY2026 guidance: revenue of $2.513–2.523bn, non-GAAP operating margin of 40.0–40.5%, unlevered free cash flow of at least $1.070bn.
overview.source: Q2 2026 earnings call: guidance and buyback (MarketBeat summary)

concentration.text: Revenue comes from 18m paying users across individuals, teams and businesses, so there is no single-customer concentration; the exposure is to the self-serve consumer and small-business base.
The real concentration is product: file sync and share, a category under pressure from Microsoft and Google bundling and from AI-native tools.

advantages.text: Cash generation: operating cash flow of $981m over twelve months and capital spending of only $23m.
A large installed base with low churn and pricing power at the margin; ARPU has held near $139 while users have grown for three straight quarters.

rationale.text: The classic buyout profile: mature, highly cash-generative, low capital intensity on the face of it, and trading at 12.5x reported EBITDA with a consensus “Sell” rating and a $31.80 average target.
Dropbox is already running a self-funded buyout of its own shares: $697m repurchased in the first half of 2026, funded partly by $1.2bn of new term loan, with a further $900m authorisation.
That makes the question sharp: can a private owner do better with the same cash flows than the public company is already doing for its shareholders?

downside.text: Revenue is flat and the product category is being commoditised. A 3% a year decline with no margin gain is the downside case.

Negative leverage: with no debt at all, the deal earns only 2.8% a year at the offer price, while the new debt costs about 9.3% (7.1% after tax). So each extra turn of debt lowers the equity return: 0.5% at the modelled 5.5x.
Finance-lease repayments of $78.7m in the first half of 2026 (data-centre equipment) are capital spending in all but name, roughly $157m a year annualised.
The 10-Q share count includes 8.27m restricted shares under the co-founder grant. If a change of control vests them, the equity cheque rises by about $376m at the offer price.
downside.source: Dropbox Form 10-Q for the quarter to 30 Jun 2026 (cover page share count)

diligence.text: How much of the $304m stock-based pay can be replaced by a management equity plan without losing engineering talent?
What are the change-of-control terms of the term loan and the 2028 convertible notes, and the vesting terms of the co-founder award?
Is paying-user growth durable once Dash and the AI integrations are priced, or is ARPU about to decline as guided?
What is the real annual cost of the data-centre lease programme over the hold?

valueCreation.text: Cost programme: reported EBITDA margin from 33.5% to 37% over five years through opex cuts (base case). Replacing most stock-based pay with a management equity plan lifts it towards 41% (upside case).
Pricing and packaging on the 18m paying users; every $1 of ARPU is about $18m of revenue.

thesis.why: A mature, cash-generative software franchise with 18m paying users, 32.8% reported EBITDA margins and about $1bn of unlevered free cash flow a year.
thesis.whyNow: The shares trade at 12.5x reported EBITDA, within a 52-week range of $21.70–38.17, with a consensus “Sell” rating. Management is already levering up to buy back stock.
thesis.wrong: The price: at a 30% premium ($47.50) the fund pays 15.4x EBITDA but can only assume an exit at today’s 12.6x, which costs more than five years of EBITDA growth adds. With no debt the deal earns 2.8% a year, below the cost of debt, so leverage makes it worse: the base case returns 0.5% a year. The highest price that clears 20% is about $24.26 a share, below today’s $36.55. Even replacing most stock-based pay only lifts that to about $28.94.

ic.marketContext: Dropbox sells cloud file storage and collaboration to 18m paying users, from individuals to businesses. The category is mature and contested: Microsoft and Google bundle storage with their productivity suites, and AI-native tools are changing how teams find and share work. Dropbox’s response is Dash, its AI search and organisation product, with broader access planned through the rest of 2026.
ic.mitigants: Underwrite on reported EBITDA, treating stock-based pay as a cash cost until a management equity plan is agreed. Treat finance-lease repayments as capital spending. Exclude operating leases from net debt, since their cost is already in EBITDA. Price the co-founder award as dilution. Size the debt to interest cover above 2x in year one, not to the maximum lenders would provide.
ic.commentary: Recommendation: pass at a 30% premium ($47.50 a share). The base case returns 0.5% and 1.02x over five years, because the fund pays 15.4x reported EBITDA but can only assume an exit at today’s 12.6x, so the multiple falls by more than flat revenue can make up. With no debt the deal would earn 2.8% a year, below the 7.1% after-tax cost of the new debt, so leverage lowers the return rather than raising it. A 20% return needs an entry price of about $24.26 a share, below today’s $36.55. The case would change with evidence of durable growth from Dash or a large, credible cost programme; without either, the public company’s own debt-funded buybacks already capture most of what a private owner could.
